Passes -XX:ActiveProcessorCount to the JVM so it sees the right core count on phones that misreport their own. Always clamped to 1-16, falling back to 8 if the device reports something bogus.
Detects this device\'s core count each launch via Runtime.availableProcessors(). Off only matters alongside Manual Override below.
Overrides Auto Detect Cores globally with the core count set below.
Used when Manual Override (or a per-instance override) is active.
Lets a specific instance\'s own CPU Core Override (set in that instance\'s Version Settings) take priority over the global pick above.
Reveals Thread Affinity and Scheduler Tuning below.
Pins the JVM\'s worker threads toward this device\'s big/performance cores instead of leaving core placement to the OS scheduler.
Hints the native side to favor steadier frame delivery over raw throughput under CPU contention.
Keeps the allocated RAM pinned to the best pick for this device instead of a value you set by hand on the Game Settings slider.
-Xms = -Xmx: reserves the full heap up front for fewer heap-resize GC pauses. Off starts the heap at half of -Xmx and lets the JVM grow it as needed.
Quick presets for the RAM slider in Game Settings.
Periodically checks the system\'s memory pressure and warns before the OS is likely to kill the game process outright.
Logs every GC pause to gc.log in the launcher cache directory, for diagnosing a slow session after the fact.
GL4ES-family renderers only (Holy GL4ES). No effect on LTW, MobileGlues, Zink, VirGL, VGPU, or Freedreno.

Sets Minecraft maxFps to 260 and disables V-Sync while enabled. Previous values are backed up and restored when disabled. Hot or battery-saving devices are not uncapped. May increase heat and battery drain.
Enables JVM string deduplication and disables shared perfdata files. String deduplication trades CPU work for memory savings; this does not enable front-buffer rendering.
Pre-touches eligible Java heaps to reduce first-access page faults. This is a memory optimization, not a renderer frame limiter; it can increase launch time and memory commitment.
Allows the renderer to drop frames when overloaded instead of queuing them. Reduces input lag on low-end devices.
Uses a balanced 50ms G1GC pause target instead of 100ms. This is a soft garbage-collection target, not a frame-time guarantee.
Periodically runs a G1 garbage collection during idle stretches to release memory back to the system, instead of holding onto peak usage all session.
Automatically tunes renderer, driver, RAM allocation, resolution scale, and FPS Boost flags for your device at launch. Recommended for most users.
Quick switch between OpenGL and Vulkan rendering. This is a shortcut for the detailed Renderer option below — OpenGL picks GL4ES, Vulkan picks Zink.
On uses the OpenGL (GL4ES) renderer. Off switches to Vulkan (Zink). Same shortcut as the detailed Renderer option below — default is On (OpenGL).

%s is a Minecraft launcher by App that allows Minecraft: Java Edition to run on Android devices.

%s focuses on optimizing user experience, redesigning the application interface, and adding more practical features, aiming to lower the barriers to play and let more people enjoy the fun of Minecraft easily.

%s uses the GPL 3.0 open-source license, which is "viral." Any code that uses, modifies, or derives from GPL libraries or software must also adopt the GPL license for open sourcing. Which CrutleAI model does what. Every job - chat, code, hard problems, images, video, voice, transcription - has its own model and its own fallback list, so one model running out of quota never takes the feature down with it. Automatic is recommended.

Each job has a list of models, best first. Crutle AI starts at the top of the list; if that model refuses the request, runs out of quota or is briefly unavailable, it silently moves to the next one and answers anyway. A model that just ran out of quota rests for a minute and a half, one that is gone for longer, so a busy minute does not waste a request on it every time.

Automatic uses the recommended list. Picking a model puts it at the front and keeps the rest as its fallback.

The model that actually answered is shown in small print under each answer in the chat.

Let\'s take a quick look at what the main screen can do.
Tap here to open the account manager, where you can add or manage your Minecraft accounts
Tap here to open the version list, where every game version you install will be listed
Not happy with where the action menu is?
Long-press the card to pick it up, then drag and drop it to dock on the other side
Don\'t worry! You can pin content here as cards and arrange it freely, as long as it provides the “%s” option
Welcome to the control layout editor!
Let\'s take a quick look at how to use it.
This is the control layout editor\'s floating menu button
Drag it to reposition it! Tap it to open the editor menu and the control layer list
This is the control layer list
A control layer works like a graphics layer: it is a container that holds controls. You can organize the controls you add by placing them on separate layers
Every control layer you add will be listed here
Tap this button to create a new control layer
Once a control layer is selected, you can add any type of control to it
Want to change how your controls look?
You can create appearances for your controls so they can be quickly reused and switched between
Use the preview mode to test out your control layout
Once you\'re done editing, remember to save your control layout!
Tap any blank area to continue to the next step
Tap any blank area to finish the guide
